Or: - To use a [keyboard shortcut](../../shortcuts.md), press Shift+i. - In the upper-right corner, select **Assigned issues** ({{< icon name="issues" >}}). ## Issue list The issue list shows all issues in your project or group. You can use it to view, sort, and manage issues. To view the issue list: 1. On the top bar, select **Search or go to** and find your project. 1. Select **Plan** > **Issues**. On the top bar, select **Search or go to** and find your project. 1. Select **Plan** > **Issues**. 1. Above the list of issues, select **Search or filter results**. 1. From the dropdown list that appears, select the attribute you want to filter by. The following filters are available: - Assignee - Author - Confidential - [Contact](../../crm/_index.md) - [Health](managing_issues.md#health-status) - Iteration - Label - Milestone - My reaction - [Organization](../../crm/_index.md) - [Parent](../../group/epics/_index.md) - Release - Search within (titles or descriptions) - Status - Subscribed - Type - Weight - [Custom fields](../../work_items/custom_fields.md) 1. Select or type the operator to use for filtering the attribute. The following operators are available: - `=`: Is - `!=`: Is not one of - `||`: Is one of (for Assignee, Author, Label, Type). Works like an inclusive OR. For example, if you filter by `Assignee is one of Sidney Jones` and `Assignee is one of Zhang Wei`, GitLab shows issues where either `Sidney`, `Zhang`, or both of them are assignees. 1. Enter the text to filter the attribute by. You can filter some attributes by **None** or **Any**. 1. Repeat this process to filter by multiple attributes. Multiple attributes are joined by a logical `AND`. 1. Press Enter or select the search icon ({{< icon name="search" >}}). #### Filter by title or description To filter the list issues for text in a title or description: 1. On the top bar, select **Search or go to** and find your project. 1. Select **Plan** > **Issues**. 1. Above the list of issues, in the **Search or filter results** text box, enter the searched phrase. 1. In the dropdown list that appears, select **Search within**, and then either **Titles** or **Descriptions**. 1. Press Enter or select the search icon ({{< icon name="search" >}}). Filtering issues uses [PostgreSQL full text search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-intro.html) to match meaningful and significant words to answer a query. For example, if you search for `I am securing information for M&A`, GitLab can return results with `securing`, `secured`, or `information` in the title or description. However, GitLab doesn't match the sentence or the words `I`, `am` or `M&A` exactly, as they aren't deemed lexically meaningful or significant. It's a limitation of PostgreSQL full text search. #### Filter issues by ID 1. On the top bar, select **Search or go to** and find your project. 1. Select **Plan** > **Issues**. 1. Above the list of issues, in the **Search or filter results** text box, type `#` followed by the issue ID. For example, enter `#362255` to return only issue 362255. 1. Select **Search for this text**. 1. Epics make complex projects manageable. They: - Break down large features into smaller deliverables that add incremental value. - Track the progress of related work items with scheduled start and end dates. - Organize discussions and decisions about feature scope and requirements. - Create hierarchical structures that connect tasks to strategic goals. - Build visual roadmaps to monitor progress toward objectives. Teams use epics to coordinate across multiple iterations and track progress toward long-term goals. In the Ultimate tier, [nested epics](manage_epics.md#multi-level-child-epics) provide additional structure through work hierarchies that align with agile frameworks. Break down complex projects into more manageable child epics, which can further contain their own sets of issues and tasks. This nested structure helps maintain clarity and ensures all aspects of a project are covered without losing sight of the overarching goals.

Ultimate only. - An epic is [linked](linked_epics.md) to one or more task, objective, or key result. "blocked by" .- KeyResult1 ``` ### Child issues from different group hierarchies You can add issues from a different group hierarchy to an epic. Select **Save changes**. ## apps/user-manuals/gitlab/user/group/epics/linked_epics.md --- stage: Plan group: Product Planning info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments title: Linked epics --- {{< details >}} - Tier: Ultimate - Offering: GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, GitLab Dedicated {{< /details >}} Linked epics are a bi-directional relationship between any two epics and appear in a block below the epic description. You can link epics in different groups. The relationship only shows up in the UI if the user can see both epics. When you try to close an epic that has open blockers, a warning is displayed. To manage linked epics through our API, see [Linked epics API](../../../api/linked_epics.md). ## Ways to use linked epics You can use linked epics to solve several planning and coordination challenges. The following examples show how linked epics help teams work together more effectively. ### Cross-functional initiatives Use linked epics to coordinate work between multiple teams and track interdependent deliverables. When teams work together on a large initiative, each team can manage their own epic while maintaining visibility into related work. For example, when launching a new feature, development and marketing teams often work in parallel. The development team tracks technical implementation in their epic, while the marketing team plans promotional activities in a separate epic. By linking these epics: - Teams can track dependencies between technical and promotional work. - Each team maintains autonomy while staying aligned on the broader initiative. - Stakeholders get visibility into the full scope of the launch. - Teams can identify and resolve blockers across organizational boundaries. This coordination helps break down silos and ensures all aspects of the initiative stay in sync. When you link epics across groups: - Each team keeps their work in their own group. - Teams can see related work without switching between groups. - Status updates automatically flow between linked epics. ### Dependency management Use linked epics to manage and track work dependencies. When development can't begin until infrastructure changes are complete, linked epics help teams manage these dependencies. For example, when building a new feature, teams often need infrastructure updates before development can start. The infrastructure team tracks their database migration work in one epic, while the development team plans feature implementation in another epic. By linking these epics: - Teams can track when infrastructure work is ready for development. - Development teams can better plan their sprint capacity. - Product managers can identify potential workflow delays. - Teams stay informed of progress without constant meetings. This visibility helps teams complete work in the right sequence and avoid blocked tasks. When you link epics to show dependencies: - Infrastructure and development work stays connected. - Teams know when they can start their work. - Status updates flow automatically between epics. ### Higher-level planning Use linked epics to connect short-term execution with long-term planning. When managing a series of releases, you can organize high-level goals and track individual feature deliverables. For example, when planning multiple releases over several quarters, you can create separate epics for each release. Then link these release epics to a central roadmap epic that tracks the overall project. By linking these epics: - Teams can understand how their work fits into the larger strategy. - Product managers can track progress across multiple releases. - Teams stay focused on current work while seeing future plans. - Stakeholders can monitor both granular and high-level progress. This structure helps teams progress on current work while maintaining broader goals. To show the sidebar again: - Repeat the previous ## apps/user-manuals/gitlab/user/group/iterations/_index.md --- stage: Plan group: Project Management info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments title: Iterations description: Time-boxed workflow, program increments, cadence, and sprints. --- {{< details >}} - Tier: Premium, Ultimate - Offering: GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, GitLab Dedicated {{< /details >}} An iteration in GitLab refers to a time-boxed workflow that groups issues to be worked on during a specific period of time, usually lasting 1-3 weeks. Teams can use iterations to track velocity and volatility metrics. For tracking the same item over multiple concurrent periods, you can use iterations with [milestones](../../project/milestones/_index.md). Create and manage various [iteration cadences](#iteration-cadences) in a group. For example, you can use: - Milestones for Program Increments, which span 8-12 weeks. - Iterations for Sprints, which span 2 weeks. In GitLab, iterations are similar to milestones, with a few differences: - Iterations are only available to groups. - Iterations are grouped into iteration cadences. - Iterations require both a start and an end date. - Iteration date ranges cannot overlap within an iteration cadence. ## Planning workflows with iterations You can use iterations to organize and track work in fixed time periods. The following examples show how iterations help teams maintain consistent delivery cycles. ### Sprint planning and execution Use iterations to plan and execute work in fixed time periods, and help teams maintain a predictable delivery cadence. When teams work in sprints, each iteration provides a clear timebox for planning, execution, and delivery of work items. For more information, see [Tutorial: Use GitLab to facilitate Scrum](../../../tutorials/scrum_events/_index.md). For example, when running two-week sprints, teams often need to coordinate multiple workstreams. The development team tracks implementation in the current sprint, while product managers prepare backlog items for upcoming sprints. By using iterations: - Teams can visualize their entire sprint schedule. - Work automatically rolls over between sprints. - Stakeholders can track sprint progress through burndown charts. - Teams can measure velocity across multiple sprints. This structure helps teams complete work consistently while maintaining visibility into progress. When you set up iterations for sprints: - Each team works in the same iteration cadence. - Teams can view work status in iteration reports. - Sprint planning becomes more predictable. ### Rapid development cycles Use iterations to support shorter development cycles when your team needs frequent releases. When practicing methodologies like Extreme Programming (XP), teams can use one-week iterations to maintain fast feedback loops. For example, when implementing rapid changes, teams might deploy to production multiple times per iteration. The team tracks their work in weekly iterations while maintaining the flexibility to release whenever code is ready. By using iterations: - Teams maintain structured timeboxes. - You can track development velocity. - Teams can adapt planning based on weekly metrics. - Stakeholders can see concrete progress each week. This approach helps teams balance agile practices with organized planning. When you use iterations for rapid cycles: - Work is organized into clear weekly boundaries. - Teams track progress in smaller increments. - Release planning aligns with iteration boundaries. ## Iteration cadences {{< history >}} - [Introduced](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/5077) in GitLab 14.1 [with a flag](../../../administration/feature_flags/_index.md), named `iteration_cadences`. Upcoming iterations are scheduled to start on the same day of the week as the changed start date. Iteration cadences can be manually managed by turning off the automatic scheduling feature. - [Generally available](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/354878) in GitLab 15.5. Feature flag `iteration_cadences` removed. {{< /history >}} Iteration cadences are containers for iterations and can be used to automate iteration scheduling. You can use them to automate creating iterations every 1, 2, 3, or 4 weeks. You can also configure iteration cadences to automatically roll over incomplete issues to the next iteration. ### Create an iteration cadence {{< history >}} - [Changed](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/343889) the minimum user role from Developer to Reporter in GitLab 15.0. - [Changed](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/169256) the minimum user role from Reporter to Planner in GitLab 17.7. {{< /history >}} Prerequisites: - You must have at least the Planner role for a group. Issues are moved at midnight in the instance time zone (UTC by default). Administrators can change the instance time zone. 1. Select **Create cadence**. The cadence list page opens. An iteration report displays a list of all the issues assigned to an iteration and their status. The report also shows a breakdown of total issues in an iteration. Open iteration reports show a summary of completed, unstarted, and in-progress issues. Closed iteration reports show the total number of issues completed by the due date. ### View an iteration report To view an iteration report: 1. Verify by confirming the parent-group label is now present on all previously tagged items.

Use the **Generate a default set of labels** button on the project Labels page to bootstrap projects that have zero labels and whose parent group also has none. This creates: `bug`, `confirmed`, `critical`, `discussion`, `documentation`, `enhancement`, `suggestion`, and `support`. The button only appears when the project has no labels, so if you don't see it, either labels already exist in the project or in an ancestor group. You need at least the Planner role.

Label priority is set only at the project level, not from the group label list. On **Manage** > **Labels**, click the star icon next to a label to prioritize it; the label then appears at the top under **Prioritized Labels**. Drag prioritized labels up and down to change relative order—higher in the list means higher priority. Priority sorting on issue and MR lists uses only the highest-priority label on each item. Verify prioritization by sorting an issue list by **Priority** or **Label priority** and confirming order.

To assign or unassign labels through the sidebar: open the item, select **Edit** in the **Labels** section, search by typing part of a label name, click labels to toggle their checkmarks, and close the picker by clicking **X** or outside the box. Sidebar label changes are visible to other users in real time on epics, incidents, issues, and merge requests without a page refresh. Alternatively use the quick actions `/label ~foo ~bar`, `/unlabel ~foo`, or `/relabel ~new` in a comment or description; verify by watching the labels appear in the sidebar after the comment posts.

The archived labels feature is behind the `labels_archive` feature flag and may not be available. When it is, archive labels via **Manage** > **Labels** > pencil edit icon > tick the **Archived** checkbox > **Save changes**. Archived labels vanish from the assign-labels dropdown but remain on items already tagged and are still searchable. Find them under the **Archived** tab on the Labels page. Unarchive by opening that tab, editing the label, and clearing the **Archived** checkbox. Archiving also deprioritizes the label automatically.

Locking a label on merge (Self-Managed, beta, flag `enforce_locked_labels_on_merge`) is done from **Manage** > **Labels** > vertical ellipsis > **Edit**, then tick **Lock label after a merge request is merged**. Warn the user first: this cannot be undone, and the label itself can no longer be deleted after being locked. Locked labels behave normally on issues and epics; the lock only takes effect once an MR carrying them is merged, at which point no one can remove them from that MR.

To create a new issue board, open the board name dropdown in the upper-left corner of the issue boards page and select **Create new board**. Provide a name and optionally scope the board by milestone, iteration, labels, assignee, or weight (scoping requires Premium/Ultimate). Once a scope is applied, you cannot filter by that same attribute in the search bar—you must first remove the scope through **Configure board** ({{settings icon}}). If you lack edit permissions you can still inspect the configuration through the same settings icon labelled **Board configuration**.

Delete an issue board by opening **Configure board** ({{settings icon}}) in the upper-right, selecting **Delete board**, then confirming with **Delete**. If the board you deleted was the last board in the project or group, GitLab automatically creates a new `Development` board so you're never left with zero boards. Verify by returning to the boards list; the deleted board should be absent and, if applicable, `Development` should appear.

Add a new list to an issue board by either selecting **New list** at the far right of the board (inserts before **Closed**) or by hovering between two existing lists and clicking the inline **New list** button that appears (inserts at that position). Choose the list type—Label, Assignee (Premium+), Milestone (Premium+), Iteration (Premium+), or Status (Premium+)—then pick the value and click **Add to board**. To reorder lists later, drag them by their headers; **Open** and **Closed** are fixed and cannot be moved.

Removing a list from an issue board only removes the view, not the underlying label, milestone, iteration, assignee, weight, or issues. Open the target list's **Edit list settings** ({{settings icon}}) at the top of the column, click **Remove list**, and confirm with **Remove list** again in the dialog. You can recreate the list at any time and the same issues will repopulate it based on their attributes.

When you drag an issue between board lists, the effect depends on source and destination. From Open to a label list adds that label; from a label A list to a label B list swaps A for B; dragging to the Closed list closes the issue; dragging from Closed back to a list reopens it and applies that list's attribute. Dragging into an assignee list assigns the user, and dragging out of an assignee list to another assignee list swaps the assignee. Verify by opening the issue's sidebar and checking labels/assignees updated accordingly.

Set a work-in-progress limit on an issue board list by opening the list's **Edit list settings** ({{settings icon}}), selecting **Edit** next to **Work in progress limit**, choosing either **Items** or **Weight** from the type dropdown, entering the maximum, and pressing **Enter** to save. The header then displays current/limit (for example **4/5**). When exceeded, the current value turns red and a divider line appears between within-limit items and excess items. Remove the limit by choosing **Remove limit**. WIP limits cannot be set on the default **Open** and **Closed** lists.

Enable epic swimlanes on an issue board by selecting **View options** ({{preferences icon}}) and choosing **Epic swimlanes**. Issues then group horizontally by their parent epic. Reassign an issue's epic by dragging its card into another epic's horizontal lane, remove it from an epic by dragging to the **Issues with no epic assigned** lane, and change both epic and list simultaneously by dragging diagonally. Verify by opening the issue and checking the Epic field in the sidebar.

To move an issue to the top or bottom of a board list without dragging through long lists, hover over the issue card, click **Card options** ({{ellipsis icon}}), and select **Move to start of list** or **Move to end of list**. This works even when filters are hiding intermediate cards—the issue still moves relative to the full list. Verify by clearing the filter and confirming the card sits at the expected end.

Focus mode on an issue board hides the surrounding navigation UI so only the board is visible. Toggle it with the **Toggle focus mode** ({{maximize icon}}) button in the upper-right corner of the board. Toggle again to restore the full navigation. Use this when demoing or when a board has many wide lists.

Ordering issues in an issue board is stored as a global relative-position value: dragging an issue above another in any board on the instance changes its rank everywhere. This affects the issues list too, and vice versa. Newly created issues receive the highest position and therefore appear at the bottom of any list. When board loading appears stuck or times out, the fix is to run `Issues::RelativePositionRebalancingService.new(project.root_namespace.all_projects).execute` from the Rails console.

Group issue boards live under the group's **Plan** > **Issue boards**. GitLab Free permits one group-level board per group, while Premium and Ultimate allow multiple. Group boards can show issues from every project in the group and its descendant subgroups. When filtering a group board: milestones from the group and its descendants are available, but only labels created directly on the group (not descendant projects) can be used in the search bar. Individual issues can still be edited to use project-level milestones and labels from their sidebars.

Status lists on issue boards (Premium+) are different from other list types: they can contain both open and closed issues depending on whether the status maps to an open or closed workflow state. When you drag an issue from a status list into an open (non-status) list, the default open status is applied automatically; dragging into a closed list applies the default closed status. Add a status list with **New list** > **Status** and select the status from the dropdown.

To create a milestone in a project or group, go to **Plan** > **Milestones** > **New milestone**. Enter a title (required) and optionally a description, start date, and due date. Both dates are optional for issues but required for a milestone to display a burndown or burnup chart. Verify the milestone is created by finding it on the milestones list; it will appear as active with its dates and percentage complete calculated as closed items divided by total items.

Milestones automatically close after their due date passes, but you can close one manually. Go to **Plan** > **Milestones**, then either use the milestone's row **Milestone actions** ({{ellipsis icon}}) > **Close**, or open the milestone and select **Close**. When a milestone is closed, its open issues remain open—they are not automatically closed with it. Verify by checking the milestone status label changed to closed and by seeing it under the Closed tab.

Promoting a project milestone to a group milestone merges all same-named project milestones across every project in the group into a single group milestone; all associated issues and MRs are transferred. This is irreversible. Trigger it from **Plan** > **Milestones**, then use **Milestone actions** ({{ellipsis icon}}) > **Promote** > **Promote Milestone**. You need at least the Planner role on the parent group. Verify by finding the milestone now listed at the group level with the aggregated issue and MR counts.

The milestone detail view has tabs: **Work Items** (Unstarted, Ongoing, Completed columns), **Merge Requests** (Work in progress, Waiting for merge, Rejected, Merged columns), **Participants**, and **Labels**. The right sidebar shows percent complete (closed items / total items), start and due dates, total time spent, total issue weight, MR counts by state, associated releases, and a copyable milestone reference. Use these views to audit milestone scope quickly without querying individual issues.

The special milestone filters, available anywhere you filter by milestone, are: **None** (items with no milestone), **Any** (items with any milestone), **Upcoming** (items with an open milestone whose start date is in the future), and **Started** (items with an open milestone whose date range overlaps today; excludes milestones lacking a defined start and due date). Use these to build views of unscheduled work or currently-active scope without naming a specific milestone.

Burndown and burnup charts only render on a milestone that has both a start date and a due date. Access them by opening the milestone from **Plan** > **Milestones**. Toggle between counting **Issues** and **Issue weight** above the chart—when using weight, ensure all issues have weights assigned or they'll be missing from the totals. Burndown shows remaining (total minus closed); burnup shows Total and Completed as separate lines so you can see scope changes (Total dropping when issues are removed) versus completion (Completed rising when issues close).

For milestones created before GitLab 13.6, the burndown chart has an additional Legacy/Fixed toggle. **Fixed** tracks full milestone history and stops counting removed issues after the due date passes. **Legacy** subtracts daily closures from daily openings and treats reopened issues as opened the day after they were last closed; changing the milestone start date changes the count of issues open on each day. Prefer Fixed for auditability; use Legacy only when reproducing historic behavior.

Assign a milestone to an issue, epic, or MR by opening the item, clicking **Edit** next to **Milestones** in the right sidebar, then searching for and selecting the milestone from both project and group options. Alternatives: the `/milestone %Sprint-3` quick action in a comment or description, dragging the issue onto a milestone list in a board, or bulk-editing from the issues list. Only one milestone can be assigned per item.

To create an issue board list based on an iteration (Premium+), select **New list** > **Iteration**, pick the iteration from the dropdown, and select **Add to board**. Changing an issue's iteration is then as simple as dragging its card between iteration lists. The list type also works with milestone and assignee lists on the same board for combined visualizations of Sprint + Assignee.

Create an iteration cadence from the group's **Plan** > **Iterations** > **New iteration cadence**. Provide title, description, and either enable automatic scheduling (requires automation start date, duration in weeks 1-4, and number of upcoming iterations) or clear **Enable automatic scheduling** to manage iterations manually. Optionally tick **Enable roll over** so incomplete issues automatically move to the next iteration at the end of each iteration (performed by the Automation Bot at midnight in the instance's time zone, UTC by default).

You can toggle automatic scheduling on and off for an iteration cadence via **Plan** > **Iterations** > cadence row's vertical ellipsis > **Edit cadence**. When turning automation on, the automation start date must not overlap any existing open (ongoing or upcoming) iteration; upcoming iterations are adjusted to fit the new schedule and additional ones are created to satisfy the upcoming-iterations count. Iterations can only be created, edited, or deleted manually while automatic scheduling is disabled.

To create an iteration manually, the cadence must have automatic scheduling turned off. Then on **Plan** > **Iterations**, next to the cadence use the vertical ellipsis menu > **Add iteration**, fill in title, start date, and due date (dates cannot overlap other iterations in the same cadence), and select **Create iteration**. Verify it appears in the cadence's iteration list.

Deleting an iteration cadence deletes every iteration inside it. Use **Plan** > **Iterations** > cadence's vertical ellipsis > **Delete cadence** > confirm with **Delete cadence**. To delete an individual iteration instead, open the iteration detail page and use the vertical ellipsis > **Delete** > **Delete**—this requires the containing cadence to have automatic scheduling turned off.

Iteration reports are viewed by opening **Plan** > **Iterations**, selecting the cadence, then the iteration. The report includes the issue list, breakdown counts (completed, unstarted, in-progress or completed-by-due-date depending on state), burndown and burnup charts. When you access the same iteration inside a subgroup or project, the counts and charts are scoped to that subgroup/project's issues only, which is useful for team-specific rollups of a group-wide iteration.

Group issues in an iteration report by label by opening the iteration and choosing **Label** from the **Group by** dropdown; then filter to specific labels in **Filter by label**. This gives per-team scope visibility inside a shared iteration. Close the label dropdown by clicking outside it to apply.

Create an epic from any of these entry points: group's **Epics** page > **New epic**; another epic's **More actions** > **New related epic** (creates linked epic); top bar **New** ({{plus icon}}) > **New epic**; or the **New epic** button in an empty roadmap. Populate title, description, confidentiality checkbox, labels, dates (or inherit), and color, then select **Create epic**.

Start and due dates on an epic can be fixed or **Inherited**. When inherited, the start date auto-updates to the earliest start date across child epics and issue milestones, and the due date to the latest such date. These values recompute automatically as children change milestones, milestones shift dates, or issues are added/removed from the epic. Because inheritance is bottom-up, changing a leaf child epic's start date can cascade all the way to the top epic.

The available epic-to-item relationships are: an epic can be the parent of issues; an epic can be the parent of child epics (Ultimate); an epic can be linked to tasks, objectives, or key results with `relates to`, `blocks`, or `is blocked by`. Child issues may come from projects outside the epic's group hierarchy—add them by pasting the issue URL through the epic's Add existing issue flow.
